name: Athaliah (mother of Ahaziah, queen)
title: Judah's only female ruler
summary: Athaliah descended from the Omride dynasty of the northern kingdom and is referred to in the biblical text as the granddaughter of Omri—likely she was the daughter of King Ahab. Through a dynastic marriage with King Joram, she became linked to the royal house of Judah and brought the Baal cult southward. When Jehu carried out his revolution and killed her son Ahaziah, Athaliah responded by seizing the throne herself and attempting to wipe out the entire Davidic royal line. For six years she ruled as Judah's only female monarch, a reign marked by idolatry and covenant-breaking. The turning point came when the high priest Jehoiada revealed that the young Joash had survived the massacre, hidden in the temple by Jehosheba. Jehoiada organized a revolt that led to Athaliah’s execution and the restoration of both the Davidic throne and the worship of Yahweh. The account highlights the tension between human ambition for power and God's preservation of David's lineage—a line that, according to the promise in 2 Sam 7, would never cease.
relatedPersons: Jehoiada the priest who guided King Joash of Judah

keyEvents.title: Marriage to Joram of Judah
keyEvents.description: Athaliah married King Joram of Judah as part of a dynastic alliance between Israel and Judah, bringing with her the worship of Baal from the religious practices of the Omride dynasty.

keyEvents.title: Extermination of the royal line
keyEvents.description: When Athaliah learned that her son Ahaziah had been killed by Jehu, she seized power by destroying nearly all the royal descendants of David's house in Judah.

keyEvents.title: Joash Saved by Jehosheba
keyEvents.description: The young prince Joash was saved from the massacre by his aunt Jehosheba, who according to Chronicles was married to the priest Jehoiada. The child was hidden in the temple for six years while Athaliah reigned.

keyEvents.title: Six Years of Reign
keyEvents.description: Athaliah ruled over Judah for six years as the only female ruler in the history of the two kingdoms and promoted the Baal cult in the land.

keyEvents.title: Jehoiada's Revolution and the Fall of Athaliah
keyEvents.description: The high priest Jehoiada organized a revolution in the seventh year, crowned the young Joash as king in the temple, and Athaliah was seized, led out, and executed at the Horse Gate.

keyEvents.title: Baal's Temple Destroyed
keyEvents.description: After Athaliah's fall, Baal's temple in Jerusalem was torn down, Baal's priest Mattan was killed, and the worship of the Lord was restored in Judah.

versions.summary: Athaliah was the daughter of King Ahab and Queen Jezebel of Israel and became the wife of King Joram of Judah. After her son's death, she seized power and nearly wiped out the entire royal line, ruling as the only female monarch over Judah for six years. She promoted Baal worship in Judah but was eventually overthrown and killed in a revolution led by the priest Jehoiada.
versions.title: Judah's Murderous Queen
versions.reason: [minor] The title 'Judean Murderess Queen' is dramatic and descriptive but may be perceived as somewhat tabloid. A more neutral title such as 'Queen of Judah' or 'Judah's Only Female Ruler' could be considered. Nevertheless, it is not incorrect.; [major] The Bible does not explicitly state that Athaliah was the daughter of Jezebel. 2 Kings 8:26 calls her 'daughter of Omri' (granddaughter/descendant), and 2 Chronicles 21:6 says Joram had 'Ahab's daughter' as his wife. It is a widespread tradition to assume that Jezebel was the mother, but this is not directly confirmed in the text. Some scholars suggest she may have been the daughter of another of Ahab's wives.; [major] Joram of Israel and Ahaziah of Israel were sons of Ahab, and thus brothers (or half-brothers) to Athaliah. Ahaziah of Israel (1 Kings 22:51) reigned before Joram of Israel. The sequence and identification are correct, but it should be noted that the Bible does not explicitly list all of Ahab's children, and the sibling relationship is a reasonable inference rather than directly stated specifically for Athaliah.; [minor] Athaliah had more roles than just 'queen'. She was also regent/ruler (she ruled actively, not merely as a queen consort) and promoter of the Baal cult. Roles such as 'regent' or 'ruler' should be added.; [minor] The summary states that Athaliah was 'daughter of King Ahab and Queen Jezebel'. As mentioned, Jezebel's motherhood is not explicitly confirmed. It is better to say 'daughter (or granddaughter) of the Omride dynasty' or 'daughter of King Ahab of Israel' without specifying Jezebel as the mother with certainty.; [minor] The event 'Baal's temple destroyed' is strictly speaking not an event in Athaliah's life, but rather a consequence of her downfall. It is nevertheless relevant to the context and can be retained.; [minor] 2 Chronicles 21:6 mentions that Joram walked in the way of the kings of Israel because he had Ahab's daughter as his wife. One could also include 2 Kings 8:18 as a parallel reference.; [major] The profile completely lacks footnotes. A profile on Athaliah should have notes about her unique position as the only female ruler in Judah/Israel, the disputed question of her origin (daughter versus granddaughter of Omri), archaeological findings related to the Omride dynasty, and theological reflections on her role in the Deuteronomistic history.

versions.summary: Athaliah was the daughter of King Ahab of Israel and belonged to the powerful Omride dynasty. She married King Joram of Judah as part of a political alliance between the two kingdoms. After her son Ahaziah was killed by Jehu, she seized power by wiping out nearly the entire royal family in Judah. She reigned for six years as the only female ruler in the history of Judah or Israel and promoted Baal worship throughout the kingdom. Her reign ended when the priest Jehoiada organized a revolution, crowned the young Joash—who had miraculously survived the massacre—as king, and had Athaliah executed. Her story highlights how the Davidic royal line was preserved through a critical threat.
versions.title: Judah's only female ruler
versions.reason: [minor] According to 2 Kgs 8:26 and 2 Chr 21:6, Athaliah is linked to the Omride dynasty, and traditionally Jezebel is regarded as her mother (as daughter of Ahab). Although this is uncertain (as the footnotes themselves discuss), one might consider setting 'mother' to 'jezebel' with a note about the uncertainty, since the summary already calls her 'daughter of King Ahab'.; [minor] The sibling list includes 'joram-of-israel' and 'ahaziah-of-israel'. According to the biblical text, Ahab had 70 sons (2 Kgs 10:1), so the list is very incomplete, but it is reasonable to include only the best-known ones. However, it should be noted that Ahaziah (of Israel) and Joram (of Israel) are the most well-attested siblings.; [minor] The summary is well written and theologically correct. A minor improvement could be to mention that she was specifically 'granddaughter of Omri' (as the biblical text states), which nuances the question of her exact familial affiliation. This makes the text more precise without losing readability.; [minor] The role 'regent' is slightly imprecise – Athaliah was not a regent in the sense of 'one who rules on behalf of another', but a self-proclaimed ruler/usurper. 'Usurper' or 'ruler' would have been more accurate.; [minor] In the event 'The Revolution and Athaliah's Fall', it states that she was executed at the 'horse gate of the king's palace'. According to 2 Kgs 11:16, she was killed at the horse entrance of the king's house. 2 Chr 23:15 says they brought her to the Horse Gate by the king's house. The description is essentially correct, but 'horse gate' is more precise than 'horse gate of the king's palace'.

versions.summary: Athaliah belonged to the powerful Omride dynasty and is referred to in the biblical text as the granddaughter of Omri, likely the daughter of King Ahab of Israel. She was married to King Joram of Judah as part of a dynastic alliance between the two kingdoms. After her son Ahaziah was killed by Jehu during his revolt against the Omride dynasty, she seized power by destroying nearly the entire royal Davidic line in Judah. As the only female ruler in the history of Judah or Israel, she reigned for six years and promoted Baal worship throughout the kingdom. Her reign ended when the high priest Jehoiada organized a successful revolt, crowned the young Joash—who had miraculously survived the massacre—as king, and ordered Athaliah to be executed. Her story highlights how the Davidic royal line was preserved through God’s providence during a critical period, despite attempts to wipe it out.
versions.title: Judah's only female ruler
versions.reason: [major] It is uncertain whether Athaliah was the sister of Joram of Israel and Ahaziah of Israel. The biblical text calls her 'granddaughter of Omri' (2 Kgs 8:26), and there is debate over whether she was the biological daughter of Ahab. Listing specific siblings as if it were established fact is problematic. Ahaziah of Israel (son of Ahaziah) and Joram of Israel are possible half-brothers, but this is not certain enough to be stated definitively as a family relationship.; [minor] That Jezebel was Athaliah's mother is a common assumption, but the biblical text explicitly states only that Athaliah was 'granddaughter of Omri'. The footnote correctly notes this uncertainty, yet the family field lists 'Jezebel' as fact. It should be considered to set mother to null or mark this with uncertainty in the summary.; [minor] The description mentions 'the Horse Gate by the king's house', but according to 2 Kgs 11:16 she was killed at the entrance of the Horse Gate by the king's house. In 2 Chr 23:15 it states that she was killed at the entrance of the Horse Gate by the king's house. The details largely agree, but the wording could be clarified slightly.; [minor] The summary is good and theologically correct, but it is quite similar in tone and structure to version 2. Since this is the third version, the phrasing should differ more from the two previous ones.

footnotes.text: Athaliah is the only woman who reigned as sovereign ruler over either Israel or Judah. Her six-year reign (c. 841–835 BC) represents a unique break in the Davidic line of succession, making her story theologically significant for understanding God's promise to the house of David (2 Sam 7).

In 2 Kings 8:26, Athaliah is called 'granddaughter of Omri' (Hebrew: bat, which can mean both daughter and female descendant). This has led to debate over whether she was a biological daughter of Ahab or perhaps a daughter from another marriage in the Omride dynasty. Some scholars have suggested she was not Jezebel's biological daughter, but this remains uncertain.

The political marriage between Athaliah and Joram of Judah reflects a well-known practice in the ancient Near East where dynastic alliances were sealed through marriage. The Omride dynasty was known throughout the region—the Assyrian Black Obelisk refers to Israel as 'House of Omri' (Bit-Humri) long after the dynasty had fallen.

Athaliah's promotion of Baal worship in Judah parallels Jezebel's role in Israel. The Deuteronomistic historian portrays both as archetypes of foreign religious influence threatening Yahweh worship, and the revolutions against them (Jehu in Israel, Jehoiada in Judah) are presented as divine intervention to protect the covenant relationship.

According to rabbinic tradition, it was a miracle that Joash survived the massacre, and his rescue is seen as confirmation of God's promise that David's line would never be cut off. The thin thread on which the messianic line hung during Athaliah's reign underscores the theme of faith in the face of seemingly impossible circumstances.

The priest Jehoiada's revolution against Athaliah (c. 835 BC) is one of the best-documented palace revolutions in ancient Israel/Judah. The detailed description of the guard rotation and military organization in 2 Kings 11:4–12 provides valuable insight into the organization of the temple guard and the interplay between the priesthood and the military power in ancient Judah.

The name Athaliah (Hebrew: עֲתַלְיָה, 'Atalyahu') likely contains the divine element -yahu (YHWH), which is remarkable for a person best known for promoting Baal worship. This may indicate that she originally received a Yahwistic name upon marrying into the Judean royal house, or that her Israelite family used YHWH-name forms despite their syncretistic practices.

Jehosheba (also called Jehoshabeath in 2 Chronicles 22:11) was, according to the books of Chronicles, married to the high priest Jehoiada. The fact that a royal princess was married to the high priest shows the close connection between the royal house and the priesthood in Judah, and explains how the temple could become a safe hiding place for the young Joash for six years.
